newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's economic success trips up on current account.
newsitem.headline: NZ's economic success trips up on current account.

text.p: New Zealand's economy, often hailed as a model for prosperity and success, hit a snag on Friday when its account with the outside world plunged to NZ$4.47 billion (US$3 billion) in the red.
It was the largest deficit New Zealand has ever recorded for its current account balance -- the difference in value between its overseas earnings and expenses.

Statistics New Zealand said the blow-out in the deficit for the year to March 31 was due to slower growth in the number of tourists visiting the country and the amount of money they spend; a fall in New Zealand's returns from offshore investments; and falling numbers of migrants to New Zealand.

The burgeoning shortfall, which is now at 4.8 percent of Gross Domestic Product, was considerably greater than economists had predicted. And with economic growth crawling at the bottom of its cycle at 1.4 percent of GDP, analysts said the current account could prove New Zealand's Achilles' heel.
"It's pretty bad. There's no two ways about it," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.

"The current account deficit is 4.8 percent of GDP when the economy is brinking on a technical recession -- it's not the kind of dynamics that I'd like to be managing," he told Reuters Financial Television.
Bankers Trust economist Nick Bennenbroek said the deficit could become a constraint on future economic growth.
"When the deficit gets large, that tends to be when investors start to become concerned that the country is continuing to spend more than it earns," he said.

"As an investor in this economy, you start think 'can this go on, is this sustainable?'. And you either want a higher return because you think there's a greater risk...or you pull out by selling your New Zealand dollar assets."
Indeed, the Kiwi dollar was sold on the news, falling about 30 pips to 66.9 U.S. cents.
That effectively loosened monetary conditions to a level which the central Reserve Bank found too hard to swallow as it tries to keep core inflation between zero and three percent.
"Overall conditions have settled too far from the Reserve Bank's desired monetary conditions," Governor Don Brash warned the markets during the afternoon after the dollar slide.
But in New Zealand's stagnant economic environment, with international speculators heavily into the money market, central bank comments have less punch than in the past.
The currency's reponse was to peek back up above 67 U.S. cents by 3.30 p.m. (0330 GMT), while bill rates dawdled just a few points lower.
Koukoulas said New Zealand's economic fundamentals suggested its currency should fall further, which would only compound the Reserve Bank's dilemma.
"With the economy being very, very weak, (and) the currency arguably being overvalued at 67 cents...there is probably more that the currency should do," he said.
However, he pointed out, if the Reserve Bank is to meet its inflation target, short-term interest rates would have to rise as the currency falls.
"But that's not consistent with their domestic settings, so I'd be a little concerned about the way the kiwi economy is panning out at the moment," Koukoulas said.
